practices.title: Agree on a family code word for emergencies
practices.summary: A secret word only your family knows beats a voice clone. Use it whenever an "emergency" call asks for money.

practices.title: Back up what you can't lose, the 3-2-1 way
practices.summary: Three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one kept somewhere else, and at least one that ransomware can't reach.
practices.time: 1 hour to set up, then automatic

practices.title: Find out what's already leaked about you
practices.summary: Check your email addresses against known breaches, then change any reused passwords that showed up.

practices.title: Freeze your credit (and your kids' credit)
practices.summary: A free credit freeze at all three bureaus stops anyone, including you, from opening new credit in your name until you lift it.

practices.title: Have the family tech talk, and keep having it
practices.summary: Agree as a family on devices, apps, sharing and what to do when something online feels wrong, with the door always open.

practices.title: Keep secrets out of code and chat
practices.summary: Passwords, API keys and tokens belong in a secrets manager, never in source code, config files, tickets or chat. Scan to catch slips.

practices.title: Learn the scam reflex, pause and verify
practices.summary: Almost every scam pushes urgency, secrecy or an unusual payment. When you feel that pressure, stop and check through a channel you already trust.
practices.time: 10 min to learn, a lifetime to practice

practices.title: Let a password manager remember for you
practices.summary: One strong password you memorize, and a different random one for every account, kept by an app that fills them in for you.
practices.time: 30 min to set up, then a few minutes a week as you log in

practices.title: Lock your screens and encrypt your devices
practices.summary: A passcode plus full-disk encryption turns a lost or stolen device from a data breach into just a lost device.
practices.time: 15 min per device (encryption runs in the background)

practices.title: Make reporting a phish easy, quick and blame-free
practices.summary: Give people one simple way to report suspicious messages, thank them every time, and act on what they send.

practices.title: Make sure you can get back into your own accounts
practices.summary: Update recovery emails and phone numbers, save backup codes, and remove old ones an ex, a former employee or a stranger could use.

practices.title: Never change payment details on the strength of an email
practices.summary: Any request to change bank details, pay a new invoice urgently or buy gift cards gets verified by calling a known number, every time.
practices.time: 30 min to write the rule, seconds to follow it

practices.title: Set up find-my-device and remote wipe before you need it
practices.summary: Turn on location and remote erase now, so a lost phone or laptop can be found, locked or wiped from any browser.

practices.title: Set up your router like you mean it
practices.summary: New admin password, strong Wi-Fi encryption, current firmware, and the risky convenience features turned off.

practices.title: Turn on automatic updates, everywhere
practices.summary: Let phones, computers, browsers, apps and routers fix their own security holes without waiting for you.

practices.title: Turn on two-step login, starting with your email
practices.summary: Add a second proof, like an app code, a security key or a passkey, so a stolen password alone isn't enough.

practices.title: Use public Wi-Fi without worrying about it
practices.summary: Modern encryption makes most public Wi-Fi fine for everyday browsing. Know the few real risks, and when to use your phone's hotspot.

practices.title: Write your "if something goes wrong" sheet, on paper
practices.summary: One page with who to call, how to reach them without your computer, and the first three things to do.

practices.title: Ask your vendors the five questions that matter
practices.summary: Before you hand a vendor your data or system access, ask a few plain questions, and keep the answers.

practices.title: Build the OWASP Top 10 habits into how you ship
practices.summary: Turn the most common web app risks into everyday habits, with checks in code review and CI instead of a once-a-year scramble.

practices.title: Close the doors you left open to the internet
practices.summary: Find what your office exposes to the internet, put remote access behind MFA, and never expose remote desktop or camera recorders directly.

practices.title: Control who can walk into your space
practices.summary: Know who holds keys, badges and codes, log visitors, and lock up network gear and paper records.

practices.title: Do a privacy checkup on your big accounts and phone
practices.summary: Walk through the privacy settings on your phone, Google, Apple, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and similar, and turn off what you didn't mean to share.
practices.time: 1 hour, once or twice a year

practices.title: Get yourself off data broker sites
practices.summary: People-search sites sell your address, phone, relatives and age to anyone. Opt out of the biggest ones, or use a service to do it for you.
practices.time: 2 to 4 hours by hand, or a paid service

practices.title: Give access on day one and take it all back on the last day
practices.summary: Use a short checklist so new people get only the access they need, and people who leave lose all of it the day they go.
practices.time: 1 hour to write, 15 min each time

practices.title: Give guests and gadgets their own Wi-Fi
practices.summary: A separate network for visitors and smart devices keeps them away from your computers and files.

practices.title: Keep admin power out of everyday accounts
practices.summary: Use a regular account for daily work and a separate, well-protected account only when you need to install, configure or manage.

practices.title: Know what you have
practices.summary: Keep a simple list of your devices, software, cloud accounts and vendors, with an owner for each. You can't protect what you don't know about.
practices.time: half a day to start, 15 min a month to keep current

practices.title: Lock down the root of your cloud account
practices.summary: Protect the AWS root user (or equivalent) with MFA and never use it, give people their own access, turn on logging and set billing alerts.

practices.title: Retire devices that can't get updates, and wipe them first
practices.summary: Replace hardware that no longer gets security updates, and properly erase anything you sell, donate or recycle.

practices.title: Run security awareness people actually remember
practices.summary: Short, real, frequent and friendly beats one annual video. Teach the why, practice the reflexes, and celebrate reporting.

practices.title: Secure your cameras and smart devices
practices.summary: Change default passwords, update firmware, turn off what you don't use, and keep cameras and smart gadgets on their own network.

practices.title: Share files on purpose, not "anyone with the link"
practices.summary: Check who can see your shared files and folders, tighten links, and set expirations for sensitive ones.

practices.title: Switch important accounts to passkeys
practices.summary: Passkeys replace passwords with a key your device holds. Nothing to remember, and nothing a fake website can steal.

practices.title: Travel light, travel locked
practices.summary: Before a trip, back up, update and lock down your devices, take only what you need, and plan for loss.

practices.title: Understand what's on the dark web about you, and what to do about it
practices.summary: The "dark web" is mostly marketplaces trading stolen logins, card numbers and personal data. Monitoring tells you what leaked. Action is what protects you.

practices.title: Practice a bad day with a tabletop exercise
practices.summary: Walk your team (or family) through a realistic scenario around a table and find the gaps before a real incident does.

practices.title: Prove your backup works by restoring from it
practices.summary: A backup you've never restored is a guess. Pick a file or a machine and bring it back on purpose.
practices.time: 30 min (a file) to half a day (a whole system)
